title: The Frozen Chosin: How Marines Survived −35°F in Korea (1950)
title_alt: You're a Marine at the Chosin Reservoir. It's 35 Below.

hook_description: Korea, November 1950. About thirty thousand UN troops, most of them US Marines, are surrounded by more than a hundred thousand Chinese soldiers at the top of a frozen mountain, at thirty-five below. Danny, a 19-year-old private, tells how they survived the cold and fought their way down one narrow road to the sea.

scenes.title: Thirty-five below
scenes.narration: Thirty-five degrees below zero. My rifle is frozen. My canteen is a block of ice. And somewhere in those hills there are more than a hundred thousand men who want us off this mountain. The only way out is one narrow road. Seventy-eight miles long.

scenes.title: Who I am
scenes.narration: My name is Danny Moore. I'm nineteen, a private in the Seventh Marines, First Marine Division. Back home in Pennsylvania, my dad works in the steel mill. I joined the Marines to see the world. I didn't know the world could get this cold.

scenes.title: Home by Christmas
scenes.narration: That November, we thought the war was almost over. We were pushing north toward the Chinese border, and the word was we'd be home by Christmas. We even got turkey for Thanksgiving. My buddy Ray said the toughest thing up north would be the mail service.

scenes.title: How we got here
scenes.narration: Here's how we got there. In June of nineteen-fifty, North Korea invaded the South. By September, we Marines had landed at Inchon, behind their lines, and the whole North Korean army fell apart. We chased them north, all the way up the peninsula. It looked like the war was won.

scenes.title: The road north
scenes.narration: Our road climbed north into the mountains, toward a frozen lake the maps called the Chosin Reservoir. One narrow dirt track, cut into the cliffs, with a drop on one side and rock on the other. Every truck, every tank, every man went up that one road.

scenes.title: The Siberian wind
scenes.narration: Then the wind came down from Siberia. The temperature dropped below zero and kept on falling. Some nights it hit thirty-five below. That's minus thirty-seven Celsius. Your breath froze on your scarf. Your eyelashes stuck together when you blinked.

scenes.title: Feet that sweat
scenes.narration: They gave us shoepacs: boots with rubber bottoms and leather tops. Great for mud. But when you marched, your feet sweated inside the rubber. And when you stopped that sweat turned to ice. That's how most of us got frostbite. Not from the snow. From our own feet.

scenes.title: Rule one: the socks
scenes.narration: So rule one: keep a dry pair of socks inside your shirt, against your chest. Every night, no matter what, you change them. The wet pair goes against your chest to dry, the dry pair goes on your feet. The guys who skipped it lost toes.

scenes.title: Never zip the bag
scenes.narration: We had good sleeping bags, thick and warm. And that was the danger. Rule two: you never zipped yourself all the way in. If trouble came in the night, you had to be out of that bag and on your rifle in a second. So we slept half-in, boots on, rifle in our arms.

scenes.title: Frozen dinner
scenes.narration: Our C-rations froze solid in the can. Beans, hash, fruit cocktail all ice. If there was a fire, we heated them. If there wasn't, we stuck the cans under our armpits and waited. Half-frozen beans for breakfast. You ate it anyway. Empty stomachs freeze faster.

scenes.title: Guns that freeze
scenes.narration: And the cold went after our weapons. Gun oil turned thick as glue. Carbines jammed. Ray's BAR fired slow, when it fired at all. So we wiped our rifles almost dry, and we worked the bolts every hour, all night long, so the metal never had a chance to freeze.

scenes.title: Ground like iron
scenes.narration: We tried to dig foxholes. The ground was frozen a foot deep, hard as iron. Our little shovels just bounced off it. So we chipped out what we could, and built up walls of rocks and packed snow around us. It wasn't much. But it was all we had between us and the wind.

scenes.title: The bugles
scenes.narration: On the night of November twenty-seventh, we heard bugles. Then whistles. Then the whole hillside came alive. The Chinese army had been hiding in those mountains for weeks, moving only at night. Now they hit us from every direction at once.

scenes.title: Fox Hill
scenes.narration: Up at Toktong Pass, one company, Fox Company, about two hundred and forty Marines, held a single hill for five days and five nights. If they had lost it, the road would have been cut, and none of us would have come home. They didn't lose it.

scenes.title: Another direction
scenes.narration: On the first of December, we started out. Our general put it in a way we never forgot: we weren't retreating. We were attacking in another direction. We loaded our wounded onto the trucks, and anybody who could still walk walked.

scenes.title: Walking at night
scenes.narration: We fought for every mile. In daylight, our planes, the Corsairs, came in low over the ridges and kept the hills clear. At night, we kept moving. If you sat down in the snow to rest, you might not get up. So you didn't sit down.

scenes.title: Across the ice
scenes.narration: On the other side of the reservoir, an Army task force had been cut off and torn apart. In the first days of December, their survivors came stumbling across the frozen lake toward Hagaru, a few at a time. Our men went out onto the ice with jeeps and sleds to bring them in. Hundreds of them made it.

scenes.title: The warming tent
scenes.narration: At Hagaru, there were warming tents with little oil stoves inside. You got a few minutes, then the next man's turn. And here's a hard lesson: if your feet were frozen, the warmth made them swell up. Men took their boots off by the stove, and then couldn't get them back on.

scenes.title: The airstrip
scenes.narration: Right there, our engineers had scraped an airstrip out of the frozen ground. Twin-engine transport planes landed on it, under fire, and carried out our wounded and frostbitten. Thousands of men flew out of that frozen field. The rest of us kept walking.

scenes.title: Tootsie Rolls
scenes.narration: And then, the strangest thing. Parachutes came down full of Tootsie Rolls. Crates of them. Nobody's ever been sure exactly why. But frozen candy was food you could thaw in your mouth. And when it was soft, it plugged holes in fuel drums. For some of us, it was the only thing we ate for days.

scenes.title: The blown bridge
scenes.narration: Below Koto-ri, the road crossed a deep gorge in the Funchilin Pass. And the bridge was gone, blown up. On one side, a cliff. On the other, a long drop. Thousands of men, and every truck and tank we had and no way across.

scenes.title: The star
scenes.narration: At Koto-ri, it snowed and snowed. Our planes couldn't fly in it. Then one night, the clouds opened and there was a single star, bright over the mountains. A lot of us took it as a sign. Today, that star is the badge of the men who came out of Chosin.

scenes.narration: We crossed that bridge in the dark, one truck at a time, with the men walking beside them in single file. Down and down the mountain, through the last ambushes, toward the sea.

scenes.title: The road behind us
scenes.narration: Behind our column came thousands of Korean families. Old men, mothers with babies on their backs, children carrying bundles bigger than they were. They walked the same frozen road, through the same cold, to get away from the war. Some of us gave them whatever food we had left.

scenes.title: Dear Mom
scenes.narration: That night, I wrote my first letter home in three weeks. I didn't tell my mother about the bugles, or the bridge, or the cold. I wrote: Dear Mom, I'm okay. Ate a hot meal today. Please send socks. Lots of socks. She sent me twelve pairs, and I gave most of them away.

scenes.title: The cold took more
scenes.narration: When they counted us up, there was a number nobody expected. More of us were carried off that mountain by the cold than by bullets. Frostbite took fingers, toes, sometimes whole feet. For the rest of their lives, a lot of the men I served with couldn't stand being cold, not even for a minute.

scenes.title: Fourteen thousand
scenes.narration: We weren't the only ones leaving. Almost a hundred thousand Korean civilians came down to that harbour, hoping for a place on a ship. One cargo ship, built for a small crew, took fourteen thousand of them on board. It sailed just before Christmas. Not one of them was lost.

scenes.title: How I survived
scenes.narration: So how did I survive Chosin? Dry socks against my chest. A rifle I never let freeze. Frozen beans, eaten anyway. Never sitting down in the snow. And a buddy named Ray, who never let me fall asleep in a foxhole.

scenes.narration: The ships took us south. We spent Christmas of nineteen-fifty in a tent camp the Marines called the Bean Patch. Years later, those of us who walked out of those mountains started calling ourselves the Chosin Few.

My name is Danny Moore, and I was one of the Chosin Few.

scenes.title: What comes next
